---
title: "desctable"
subtitle: "Stata command for descriptive statistics tables"
---
<<dd_version: 2>>

`desctable` creates formatted descriptive statistics tables using Stata.
The table is automatically exported to Excel, where it can be easily copied
and pasted to Word without losing the formatting. `desctable` treats
continuous, binary, and nominal variables differently -- providing
formatting, labeling, and statistics that are most appropriate for the
measurement level of each variable. Binary and nominal variables are
entered with the `i.` prefix; variables without a prefix are treated as
continuous. Rows are labeled with the variable labels, and the categories
of nominal variables with their value labels, so a well-labeled dataset
produces a table that needs no further editing.

## Installation

```stata
net install desctable, from("https://tdmize.github.io/data") replace
```

To read the help file in Stata, type `help desctable`; it is also
[on this site](help.html). `desctable` uses `putexcel`, so Stata 14.1 or
newer is required.

## Citation

In general, I do not think the use of `desctable` requires citation. So for
most cases, feel free to use `desctable` without citation. But, if you
need or want a citation you can cite `desctable` as:

> Mize, Trenton D. and Bianca Manago. 2018. "desctable: Stata command for
> descriptive statistics tables."
> <https://www.trentonmize.com/software/desctable>

## Examples

The examples use Stata's `nlsw88` data. `filename()` is the only required
option: it names the Excel file that the table is written to. The default
table reports the mean (the proportion for binary and nominal variables)
and the standard deviation of the continuous variables.

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
sysuse nlsw88, clear
desctable wage age i.race i.union i.collgrad tenure i.occupation hours, ///
    filename("descriptivesEX1")
<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/desctable-ex1.png){width=45% fig-alt="Default desctable output opened in Excel: a table titled Descriptive Statistics (N = 2246) with Mean and SD columns; race and occupation categories are indented under their variable labels, and SD is blank for the binary and nominal rows."}

`stats()` chooses the statistics and their order. Frequencies are reported
for the categories of nominal variables, and the minimum, maximum,
interquartile range, and median for continuous variables:

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
desctable wage age i.race i.union i.collgrad tenure i.occupation hours, ///
    filename("descriptivesEX2") stats(mean freq sd min max iqr median)
<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/desctable-ex2.png){width=85% fig-alt="desctable output with Mean, Freq., SD, Min., Max., IQR, and Median columns; the frequencies fill only the category rows, and the continuous statistics only the continuous rows."}

`group()` reports the statistics separately for each category of a nominal
grouping variable, side by side:

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
desctable wage age i.union i.collgrad tenure i.occupation hours, ///
    filename("descriptivesEX5") group(race)
<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/desctable-ex5.png){width=80% fig-alt="desctable output with Mean and SD columns for each of three race groups, white, black, and other, under a shared title."}

The [help file](help.html) lists the other options: the full set of
available statistics (including survey-weighted and multiple-imputation
means), `decimals()`, `listwise`, `notes()`, `title()`, and the font and
layout settings. The [help-file examples](help-examples.html) run several
of them.
